utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Mico Stanisic is represented today by Ms. Whittaker and Slobodan Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a matter which has been brought to the attention of the Judges and I don't know whether there is going to be a formal application made by -- I assume it's the Prosecution today about the apportionment of time today, or am I being premature?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can raise it formally. Ms. Pidwell had raised it informally because of a shortage of time. It is in the hopes of being able to finish the next witness today so that he doesn't have to stay over the long weekend, and because we have a videolink scheduled for Monday, we were hoping if we could have an extra session today we might be able to finish the upcoming witness as well as this one. I know Mr. Olmsted has some discussions with the Defence about how long they anticipate further cross on this witness. I think Mr. Aleksic said he needed probably no more than one session. The Stanisic team indicated they may have no questions. Mr. Olmsted then has 15 to 30 minutes. Ms. Pidwell said maybe one session and I don't know how much the Defence has for the second session. But that's the hope and that's what I have been asked to bring to your attention and make a request, if we could have an extended sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regarding the coming witness, ST-258, our initial estimate was based on the Prosecution's estimate. It was first three hours and then after we got the interview of that witness, the English transcript, I said we would need not more than one session. However, we received last night the proofing notes, where the witness changed his story entirely regarding certain facts as compared to the interview. So I'm not sure any longer that we could do the cross-examination in just one session, although I'll try. And we also received the motion for protective measures for the same witness, from which we see that the Prosecution intends to lead this witness regarding facts completely different than the adjudicated ones, so I will certainly take longer in examining him than I had planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you mentioned something by the way about a videolink for Monday. Could you remind me as to what time that is set for? The reason why I'm asking is that the latest version of the calendar that has been published doesn't indicate that we are sitting on Monday. Could you remind me as to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding that Monday we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon, partly because the witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I now remember that. Yes, yes, yes, yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to Mr. Krgovic has said and maybe I can make a suggestion that we inquired to see if there is availability of a courtroom and as we progress this morning, maybe at the end of this session or at the end of the second session, we will have a better idea whether there is any possibility to do it. If it appears it is impossible, then I guess you can make that decision at the time. But -- I just suggest that maybe we keep an open mind and if there is a room available we can have it on stand by, in case that might work out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At least we're all on notice. Thanks. Good morning, Mr. Witness. The -- I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, having benefitted from your lengthy introduction yesterday, we look forward to your continuation of your cross-examination proper this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you, during the proofing for this case, did you have the opportunity to re-listen to your evidence in other cases?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a small part of it, because the -- the material is vast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly on the subject of distribution of power, division of power in Prijedor. In the Kovacevic case on pages 366 to 370, you said that one of the pre-election promises of the SDA was that, ultimately, a Muslim would be elected chief of police, that is, head of the SUP, which met with the opposition of the SDS, because their candidate, as you said, was Simo Miskovic. And, furthermore, you said that problem, that issue, was resolved to the advantage of the SDA with the appointment of Mr. Hasan Kolondjic [phoen] as chief of the police of Prijedor, and then you said in lines 1 to 6, page 368: [In English] "But, of course, it was only after very long and difficult negotiations and it was in consultation with our central party boards SDA and SDS, respectively. And in the end, the SDS had to accept the principles that been agreed upon at the level of the republic." [Interpretation] Also, on page 369 in the same case you said: [In English] "Everything that happened at the level of the republic was then transferred to the level of the municipality. This was especially the case with the SDS, and when it comes to Prijedor, the SDS did not fully follow the directives from the SDS office in Sarajevo. Very often they would block the implementation of certain things for which they had orders." [Interpretation] Do you remember giving this evidence? Mr. Sejmenovic, do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I remember. I agree with the quotations you've read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the same case, probably in cross-examination, you were asked about the same thing. And then you said: [In English] "Yes, and after that, the leadership of the SDS and SDA agreed in Prijedor," in Prijedor, probably, "to divide this post in such a way. But I did say that this was done only after the intervention, after the urging from the leaders of the republic level, as far as I remember, because I was not present. But I know that this was the only way to solve the problem because SDS did not agree at the local level to completion [sic] of the allocation of power in this manner." [Interpretation] Finally, you said that you personally put that problem forward in Sarajevo, and then you said, Mr. Kadiric, said, Let them have this position. Let their man have it.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We're talking all the time about Mr. Talundzic. Ultimately, the Municipal Board of the SDS, after the intercession from their headquarters, agreed that Mr. Talundzic take that post.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Kadiric is not from the SDS. You said Kadiric said, Let their man have it. Kadiric was from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Quite correct. It was a conversation between Mr. Srdjo Srdic and Mr. Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 2D02-2121.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, this exhibit was shown to you previous in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, can we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 27. I'm sorry. If we have the body of the text enlarged, that's a conclusion in the middle. In B/C/S, can we zoom in on the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this exhibit being shown to you? It's a part of a large exhibit of the Prosecution in the Brdjanin case. It's one page from the Official Gazette in Prijedor. And in this conclusion, number 116, it says: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality does not accept and considers as invalid any and all decisions by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted before 22nd June 1992." And then point 2: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality shall implement all the enactments submitted to it and adopted after 22nd June 1992 by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." And just one more document and then I'll put you the -- put to you my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 2D02-2122; tab 28. This is the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This is another conclusion of the same Crisis Staff of Prijedor made two days later where they say: "The Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff shall not apply any enactments adopted by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina until such time as the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has re-elected all members of the government in a manner ensuring equal representation of all municipalities through the election of their candidates to the government." Now my question, Mr. Sejmenovic: Bearing in mind in your earlier evidence in the Kovacevic and other cases, as to the behaviour of the local SDS towards the headquarters, it follows from these documents that they did perhaps not as they pleased but they decide autonomously what they would and wouldn't apply and they were rather pig-headed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir. These were two entirely different periods with entirely two different presidents of the SDS. In the first time, after the election, the president was Mr. Srdjo Srdic. We had co-operation with them in certain periods. It was even good. While Srdic was receiving criticism from the level of SDS in Sarajevo and criticism from the local level saying that Srdjo Srdic was not pushing their political agenda quicker. I inquired about certain of these things. And because Srdjo Srdic was not pushing the political agenda of the SDS fast enough, he was replaced and Simo Miskovic was elected in his place. That's about the -- that level. As for the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the authorities in that region were in a certain kind of conflict with other authorities. I know that some time after this period, even Kupresanin was replaced from his position, and around that time, the autonomous regions were abolished completely. Something else was established in their place. And jurisdiction was given to local levels and other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said something similar answering the questions of Mr. Ackerman in the Brdjanin case. You said it looked like a struggle for power in the area of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Prijedor. In Prijedor, in fact, the power of the SDS was firm, powerful and untouchable. There was no competition at all, no rivalry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we are not on the page sage, Mr. Sejmenovic. I meant the Serbian authorities in Prijedor and the Serbian authorities in Banja Luka. I'm talking about that struggle for power. Because they are saying, We are not going to apply your decisions until you elect our representatives to the government.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that from these documents. But I'm trying to say that it was a time when the whole government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was falling apart. What their political relationships were, I don't know. But I know that all formal, legal relations functioned impeccably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On this subject another few questions. You talked yesterday and earlier about that meeting in Banja Luka which was supposed to take place in September, including Mr. Karadzic and international representatives, and you mentioned in your earlier evidence that, on that occasion, you saw Mr. Srdjo Srdic who was furious and yelling.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And he said that he was furious that all the power was given to presidents of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, local power that related to municipalities. Now, what was behind it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And the regions were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the regions were abolished by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we get exhibit numbers for these two documents that the witness discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't mind the line of questioning. They certainly can put their case to this witness. But this witness would be completely unfamiliar with these decisions. He hasn't even been asked whether he was aware that these two decisions were even issued. He wasn't a member of the Serb Crisis Staff during this time period. He was in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, if we are going to apply that principle, then this witness talked about many things, and yesterday he discussed a document of the 5th of July, which Simo Drljaca sent to the CSB Banja Luka. He has certain knowledge. He commented on the document. He said he was aware of it. He spoke about the meeting in Banja Luka, which had to do with the fact that all the power was vested in presidents of the municipalities, and from this document, it follows precisely that it was a tug of war between Serbs, between local officials and -- and those in Sarajevo and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On a different tact, Mr. Aleksic, I notice that both of these items are excerpts from the Official Gazette. Correct me if I'm wrong, but wouldn't the gazette form part of the law library?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think this part is. It's an Official Gazette of Prijedor municipality. And these two or three sheets are part of a large Prosecution exhibit from the Brdjanin case. I'm not sure it's in our law library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, it mightn't be in the law library. I'm asking whether -- assuming that it is something that is relevant for our purposes whether because it an is excerpt from the Official Gazette whether it should not be -- rather than exceptionally exhibited, be part of the law library, that's the question I'm asking. I can't recall as I sit here how we have dealt with other items from the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But this was a local decision of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. As far as I understand things, the law library includes documents from the republic level and the federal level, from the times of the SFRY, laws, decrees, bylaws; but this is a specific conclusion of the municipal assembly. I don't think it's in the law library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You had something to say, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My objection was aimed at the fact that this is not the appropriate witness to admit these particular decisions because no foundation was established. However, if Your Honours believe it is something that should go into the law library, the Prosecution doesn't object on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, that was a question that I raised because as I said, I observed that it was part of the Official Gazette, but counsel has pointed out that heretofore we have not included within our concept of the law library -- what shall I call -- regional bits of official documents, if I may call them that. We have confined it to, shall I say, national bits of material. So -- so -- this is not -- if we were to include this in the law library it would not be consistent with what we had done previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that we have, Your Honours, included some, at least, regional material. I think the ARK Crisis Staff Official Gazettes are in the law library. I would have to confirm that with our law library expert. But at any rate, the Prosecution would take the position that there's no reason to draw a distinction between something at the national level or the regional level or the municipal level. If it is an Official Gazette document, it seems that it falls within the scope of the law light library. We certainly would want to be using these kind of documents. We have been using them and want to use them during the Defence's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have just been alerted that this document is in the law library, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The one we are looking right now is definitely in the law library. We can let you know in a minute with regard to the second one. Yes, Your Honour, both are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I finish my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have enough time. Please bear with me. We have quite a few other subjects to cover. Mr. Sejmenovic, you knew Mr. Simo Drljaca before the events of 30 April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, on pages 45581-82, Ms. Korner was examining you, and she showed you a document which was a dispatch of 30 April sent by Mr. Simo Drljaca. I won't show you that same document now. And she asked you the following: "[In English] Before the 13th of April, had you come across Simo Drljaca? "A. I only saw him several times. I knew him by sight. I did not have any direct contact with him, by virtue of my function. I did contact with Mr. Talundzic but I did not have any such contact with Mr. Simo Drljaca, but I did knew -- know him. I saw him several times."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct, this, that I just read?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I knew him. In our language, "knowing somebody" means meeting him, talking to him. Now, whether I'd seen him, whether I would recognise him is a different issue. Of course, I saw him a few times, but I never contacted with him. For example, I don't know your colleague, but I've seen him. So it's correct what I said. I did see him on a few occasions, but I never had any contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But you knew what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a very unique voice, and I sort of knew what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the same case, in the Stakic case, on page 4772, you were shown a video, and the video said the following: That Mr. Simo Drljaca was explaining the situation to foreign journalists. So Ms. Korner said: "Could we stop the tape for a minute." And asked you the following? [In English] "Mr. Sejmenovic, Simo Drljaca that we see there talking to the foreign journalist, had you seen him at the camp before that? This is in Omarska." [Interpretation] She was referring to Omarska. You replied: [In English] "No, I had not, not before that. "Q. Did you actually know Simo Drljaca? "A. I knew that he was with the police. I saw him several times on various occasions, but I did have -- didn't have any direct contact with him." [Interpretation] This was in 2002, when you were shown this video. And when you knew both his name and you knew what Simo Drljaca looked like; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is identical to what you read out a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Four years before that, in 1998, in the Kovacevic case, you were shown the same video, and on page 567, the question was on page 566,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY ASKED
utterances.text: [In English] "Who was the man on the tape?" [Interpretation] And you replied: [In English] "This is Mr. Simo Drljaca." [Interpretation] That was in 1998. And then on the next page, it was the same video, just a little further on in the footage. The Prosecutor asked you whether you can recognise the person who was in the middle of the still. And you said: [In English] "Yes, it was Simo Drljaca, the police chief in Prijedor." [Interpretation] In the same case, the Kovacevic case, similarly to all other cases, you testified about the meeting that was held with the SDS leadership in mid-May. So on pages 422 to 427 in the Kovacevic case you were asked who was present at that meeting. And you said: [In English] "From the SDA, Becir Medunjanin attended the meeting, Mr. Islam Bahonjic, Mr. Meho Tursic, Mr. Ilijaz Music and myself." [Interpretation] And then on the next page you said: [In English] "In that office, in addition to Mr. Miskovic, was Mr. Dusan Kurnoga, Slobodan Kuruzovic, then an angry woman. I had never seen her before. I don't remember her name. And then another -- another or two people, I cannot state their names at this point." [Interpretation] And then you were asked whether the meeting started immediately and you said that you had to wait for Zeljaja and Arsic to arrive. All that happened on the 8th of July, 1998. Then in the same case, five days later, you were cross-examined and you were asked who was present at these meetings. You said the following: [In English] "The officials at that meeting didn't speak much. Slobodan spoke, and Mr. Simo as well." [Interpretation] And then on page 626, you said: [In English] "... half an hour later, Mr. Zeljaja and Arsic and another soldier or a military officer who you did not know arrived; isn't that correct? "A. Yes." "Q. Did anyone else arrive with them? "A. I don't remember whether anyone else arrived with them. There were some persons present there previously and I had mentioned them." [Interpretation] On the next page, you said: [In English] "I already stated that Kuruzovic was present as well as Miskovic. Dusan Kurnoga was present and there were another one or two persons whom I did not know. They were in civilian clothes. I assume that they were not members from the SDS leadership," [Interpretation] and so on. Do you remember that being your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, could you just help us out. Which of the denied adjudicated facts does this -- all of this concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this relates to the fact that both the police, the army, and the SDS acted practically together. And the police forces also participated in the attack on Kozarac. This was the meeting that preceded that. And this is a part of this witness's evidence that he mentioned for the first time after 18 years; namely, that Mr. Simo Drljaca was at that meeting. If the Chamber is of the opinion that I needn't challenge the witness's testimony in that regard, I will move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to be sure that we are keeping ourselves within the limits of the denied adjudicated facts. And I'm still not sure that this is the case, but let's hear Mr. Olmsted. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's not in dispute that this witness, in his prior testimony, was not able to identify Simo Drljaca at this mid-May 1992 meeting with Simo Miskovic and others. He said that there was two people who were not identified, so the issue here with regard to identity is whether he was subsequently able to identify that person at the meeting. And this hasn't been put to him yet, and I think that is the point that needs to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the point of me asking that question? What's the point of that? I started reading to the witness his testimony of 12 years ago and eight years ago. He was then shown the same video and he knew who Simo Drljaca was, what he looked like, and what his name was. He testified for three weeks in the Stakic case. And the video was shown again and the meeting was discussed again, and yesterday he said that he was introduced as an official of public security. He'd never used that term before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A security officer, not from public security. There were two security officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Military?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military security man, Arsic called him, My security officer. And those other two men were called security officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, but this is something completely new now.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I won't get into arguments with you. Don't assist me. I will ask you the questions, if the Chamber will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to know in everything that has been read to you as your prior testimony, that, at one point, if the reading was more or less complete, at one point you named the name of Simo, nothing else. Right, Mr. Aleksic? What -- what did you mean by Simo, or who did you point out by Simo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, every time, and in every case, when I was asked about this, I listed the names of people whom I knew and whom I'd had contacts with. There were people there who I didn't know. And some of them were introduced as security officers. One of them who was sitting next to Major Zeljaja was called, My security officer by Arsic. He was from military security. As for the people who I didn't know, I merely mentioned them as being present at the meeting and I said that they spoke. However, one of these people reminded me very much, because of his unique voice and his hair, of a person whom I later saw on that tape. I didn't know Simo Drljaca personally. I had seen him on a few occasions. I sometimes saw him in civilian clothes. I sometimes saw him in police uniform. And he looked somewhat different in a military uniform from how he looked in civilian clothes. With a certain degree of certainty, I said that I assumed that this was Simo Drljaca. That was my reply. I wasn't decisive and said, Yes, Simo Drljaca was present. My opinion is that that was him, except I didn't know the man personally, so I couldn't say, Yes, that was Simo. That's what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: One other question on this issue. But as I said, it was 12 and eight years ago, respectively, that you were shown the video footage. And in the past couple of days, you never said that, yes, it was Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't dare to do so even now. I wouldn't dare say, yes, this is Simo Drljaca. I know that it was a man from public security, and, based on the footage that I was able to see later on, the individual reminded me of Simo Drljaca. What we need to draw a distinction between a resolute statement without a doubt or -- or uncertainty and a statement which isn't certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, 4609 is the page, you were asked: [In English] "You say that Miskovic refused to start without the military being there. Did the officers, Arsic and Zeljaja arrive?" [Interpretation] Your answer is: [In English] "Arsic, Zeljaja and two other officers arrived, four all together. "Q. Did you know who those two other officers are? "A. No, I had never seen them before. One spoke in the Ekavian dialect which means that he was not from Prijedor but from Serbia proper. And he was the chief of security. At least that's how he was introduced by Colonel Arsic, chief of Security Service or Intelligence Service." [Interpretation] At the end of page, you were asked about the fourth officer. Both the third and fourth, that is: [In English] "And what was the security officer? Did you see what rank he was -- what rank he was? "A. I don't remember seeing a rank but it's possible that he was a major. "Q. And the other officer, was he introduced in any particular way? "A. The other officer was not introduced. He never said a word." [Interpretation] It follows from this, that it was yesterday that you mentioned for the first time a person from public security and we understand that you weren't sure if it was Simo Drljaca or not.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to answer. There were security officers present, and Arsic, a military commander, referred to one of them as his security man. So they were security officers, one of whom was Arsic's. I don't know who the other ones belonged to. And let me tell you one other thing: When they stepped into the room, they all looked the same to me. They all wore camouflage uniforms. I didn't pay attention to any details. I was focussed on the substance and the discussion at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, let me try to expedite my examination. As for the uniforms and insignia worn by these armed men - let us call them that - you testified on this score in several cases. It was for the first time yesterday, 18 years later, 18 years after the events and eight years after your testimony on this, that you mentioned that some of theme wore blue police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true, but you are entitled to your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I object to the question, because it is very vague and ambiguous. Which men wearing which uniforms at what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take it step by step then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You referred to the period after the attack on Kozarac and said that you personally observed the movement and actions taken by Serb soldiers, as you called it. In the Tadic case, page 938, you said: [In English] "Some of them were uniformed completely, some of them wore jeans and a military shirt above it. Some were younger, some were older. I recognised one of these younger soldiers. I heard some of them, two of them, I heard talking in an accent or dialect which does not come from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I guess that were young soldiers from Serbia because did how they -- dialect was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Q. Did you see any of the insignias of the uniforms of any of these soldiers or paramilitary troops? "A. They buried -- they were some without any insignias. Some had insignia of the Serbia army, some had insignia which I don't really distinguish them. Those from Vukovar had insignia of the so-called Martic Militia, this army, there were all sorts of them. [Interpretation] In the Kovacevic case, 527 --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I give you my comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Wait for me to finish and then I will put my question to you. So I have already put it to you that your testimonies differ. So in the Kovacevic case, 527: [In English] "Q. I could -- how were you able to tell that that are Serbian forces? "A. I could conclude that based on the insignia. I watched them from a short distance. I was hiding in the grass or the bushes by the road and I also knew it because one of the Ukrainians that I have mentioned, in order not to be shot, has forced to put on the uniform and become a member of the Serbian army. He gave some information." [Interpretation] Page 529 to 530 you say: [In English] "I saw few soldiers. They had insignia, two or three types of insignia. The police of region of Krajina, they were -- was the JNA insignia and also some insignia I hadn't seen until that time. I saw mixed groups. Some of them had the full uniform on. Some wore jeans and military-type shirt. There were people who were younger, some were older, and I list them in conversation which -- what strange to me." [Interpretation] And you again referred to the Ekavian dialect or accent. In the Stakic case, again you say: [In English] "I saw soldiers carrying the SAO Krajina insignia or Martic police, as they were referred to at that moment. There were regular JNA soldiers too. There were police officers from Prijedor who were soldiers. They were wearing soldier military uniforms. They were civilians, too, from neighbours recognised those civilians wore military uniforms or parts of military uniforms. That was a mixture of everything." [Interpretation] Yesterday, you said that you saw three groups of soldiers, one group was wearing complete uniforms; the second group had ten soldiers among them and two wearing dark blue police uniforms; and the second -- the third group, you said, was a mixed one comprising persons who had full uniforms and partial uniforms. Can you tell Their Honours which is the interpretation you stand by?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by each and every one. These were answers to the specific questions that were put to me which were similar questions but not identical. Sir, you need to distinguish between the various locations I was describing. I already told you that I was able to observe these events on three occasions. On three occasions. You were now referring to the contradiction in the description of the ethnic cleansing at two different locations. And they differed. I could explain and describe to you each and every one of these occasions but it would take some time. Now, the first example you mentioned, and I'm quoting you, as you were quoting to me, that there were uniformed individuals, save for some others. Well, to me, anything other than uniform was a -- were -- was civilian clothes. I wasn't even describing those who weren't in uniforms. I said that some wore full uniforms, others only parts of uniforms. The second occasion involved APCs -- or, rather, that was the last occasion when I was observing a specific location and there I saw mixed uniforms. My answer would largely depend on the person putting the question and the persons intention of inquiring after details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic. Did you know that in the Prijedor public security station on the 29th of April, a meeting was held, attended by Mr. Cehajic, the president of the municipality; Mr. Mujadzic, SDA president; and Mr. Simo Miskovic from the SDS. They met with the chief of police, Talundzic. Were you informed of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up Exhibit 1D150.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On this issue, you testified in the other cases as well, that, if I remember correctly, on the 8th of April, orders or instructions came from the Republican Territorial Defence Staff concerning mobilisation of TO units. Do you recall that? We will come to the document later. Please answer my question first.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that a Republican TO Staff was set up. I don't recall what sort of an order was issued. I recall that later on there followed an order on mobilisation, whether it was dated on the 8th of April, is not something I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the B/C/S version be somewhat enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The order was sent by Mr. Alija Delimustafic to all public security stations on the 29th of April. Through this order, he is basically conveying Mr. Hasan Efendic's order, he was the commander of the Republican TO Staff, wherein Mr. Delimustafic orders, under 1: "All roads in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina being used by units of the former JNA for pulling out materiel and equipment are to be completely blocked in direct co-ordination with the Ministry of Interior." Under 2: "Larger areas with military installations from which they are trying to pull out materiel and equipment are to be blocked by using various man-made and natural obstacles which will shall be guarded by the units of the Territorial Defence of the republic of BH and the MUP." And under 3: "Unannounced convoys of former JNA units and convoys without a MUP escort shall not be allowed to leave the barracks or to communicate within the territory of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Were you familiar with Mr. Delimustafic's order?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your earlier question, you used a term which is not appropriate for this document. Mobilisation of the Territorial Defence is one thing, and operative orders, such as this one, are quite another matter. The republic had issued orders for additional mobilisation of Territorial Defence earlier on; whereas, this particular order is an order on activities to be carried out. The command of the municipality of Prijedor TO Staff was in Prijedor. The makeup was mixed in terms of ethnicities and political parties. At the level of Prijedor, not even an order on the mobilisation of the TO could be implemented because of the obstructions that existed within the TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, this order, however, states that through various man-made and natural obstacles, which are to be secured by the TO and the MUP. So this involves both the TO and MUP units. Were you familiar with an order of this sort?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed of this particular order. But I was familiar with the fact that - and you will agree with me - an -- a combat order cannot be issued to a Territorial Defence structure that had not been previously mobilised. This is what concerns the TO. Now, the MUP operated the way it did. This order could definitely not have been implemented, to my knowledge, either through official structures or otherwise, because the local policy was heading in quite a different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm telling you is that this dispatch by Mr. Delimustafic and a similar order by Mr. Hasan Efendic were, in fact, the reason why the takeover took place in the Prijedor on the 30th of April. Will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't give you a yes-or-no answer, sir. I can't. Several towns had, by that time, been burned in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the time the dispatch was issued. Massacres occurred. That's one thing. There were cannons around Prijedor. Battery positions were placed around Kozarac much earlier than the order itself was issued. So this could have been used as a motive for something, because the SDS authorities knew well what the position of the TO was. The fact of the -- a fact of the matter is that the SUP chief, Hasan Talundzic, did not carry out this particular order de facto and de jure. He could have produced immediately an order based on this one. Why? Well, because there was no intention of having this implemented in Prijedor, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And were you at this meeting on 29th of April in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But I didn't have this document either, and you're asking me about the document. So I am fully entitled to speak to this document as well and the time-period involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As regards the Territorial Defence, in addition to what you said, that in early April, the republic staff ordered the mobilisation of TO units, in the Tadic case you said there had been constant communication between the republic TO staff and local staffs and that a decision was made also in Kozarac to re-enforce the TO. Then the Presiding Judge asked you when that decision was taken. And on page 975, you answered that it was seven or ten days before the meeting in Prijedor, which was in mid-May. Do you remember testifying to this?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After the meeting in Prijedor held in mid-May, as you said, you testified in other cases and here that meetings were held in the local commune and that a meeting was held in the school-house in Kozarac, the primary school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were also asked on page 647 and 648 in Kovacevic case: [In English] "The purpose of the meeting was to have a large number of people make a common decision that would be supported by everybody." [Interpretation] You were asked: [In English] "How was the decision reached at the meeting and what was the decision? "A. The decision at the meeting was for us to abide by the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we did not recognise the state that was created by the Serbs. Decision was made to follow the instructions of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and our authorities." [Interpretation] To avoid going through your extensive testimony in the Stakic case and others, you have been asked many questions here about the Territorial Defence, the local defence in Kozarac. But you answered most of them by saying that you didn't know that you have no such information. You said you didn't know how many establishment TO units there were in Kozarac and around. You don't know how many men these units had. You don't know how many policemen, in total, there were at the police station in Kozarac, or what kind of weapons and how many weapons had. And you didn't know who the wartime commander was in Kozarac. And that you don't know, because you were not part of the command structure in Kozarac, but you signed up as a regular citizen. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Sead Cirkin is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sead Cirkin was appointed -- or, rather, took over the organisation of the Territorial Defence just before the war started. I think it was very little time before the attack. He was a former JNA officer who was demobilised after being wounded, returned home to Kozarac, and then he was engaged to do this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was the TO commander in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please. Perhaps he was at that moment when he took over that work, but until then, no. Until that time, it was someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Who was that someone else before Cirkin, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of several people. It could have been one of them. I -- I can't say. I'm afraid to make a mistake. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Last Friday and yesterday you mentioned a tank that was placed at the intersection just before entering Kozarac. And you said at page 17386 that the tank was placed there towards the end of April and remained there until the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an approximate time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please wait. I'll give you time to answer. In Kovacevic on page 498, you said the tank was placed there on 3rd May 1992 and stayed there for a few days. And on page 643, you said that at the time when the tank was placed there, the local population from the other side of the road set up a check-point as some sort of protection. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps at that time I remembered the exact date. This time around, I find it more difficult to remember dates. But I know that when the tank was brought and the barrel of the gun was trained at houses, I know that local residents placed logs on the road so that if the tank were to move, it couldn't move so easily towards the settlement. The tank remained there for a while, and then it was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday if you knew that, on the 24th of May, the military column in Jakupovici was attacked, and you said you doubt that that was true, precisely because the tank was in that intersection from the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be a mistake, and I will ask for the audio recording, because I didn't say that. Because it's impossible to associate these two locations. There must be a distance of 6, 7 kilometres between them. What I can tell you and what is related is this: When the tank was placed there, it created a lot of fear. That fear remained. And perhaps what happened in Jakupovici was a result of that fear. And a big question is whether this tank arrived firing or -- or not. And even that event in Jakupovici, I only heard stories about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In early evidence, and yesterday as well, you said that after the 30th of April you had no contact with the SDA leadership. I mean Mr. Mujadzic and the part of the leadership who --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some of them I did; with others, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You don't know if he had any negotiations with Mr. Miskovic after the 30th of April, and if he did, what kind?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You also testified that in other villages on the other side of Prijedor - Hambarine, Carakovo, Ljubija, Rizvanovici, Biscani - they had Territorial Defence, but since they were on the other side of Prijedor, more than 10 kilometres away, you don't know what happened there after the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard news from the radio and we could see with our own eyes what happened when the artillery started targeted that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Edo Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Edo; but I know Veso Sadikovic, the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Slavko Ecimovic from Carakovo is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Zivko Ecim. I don't know Slavko Ecimovic but I know Zivko lived there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslim forces attacked Prijedor town on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from Serbian sources, the Serbian radio and their police communications, and that's the only interpretation of events I heard. I was unable to hear the other side of the story at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I quite understand. You also testified that after the 30th of April, you don't know what happened in Prijedor itself. You attended these meetings twice, but you did not leave in Prijedor. You were in Trnopolje and Kozarac on that side where you were in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you about the details and the atmosphere in Prijedor from that day when I went there. Otherwise, I was not there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I will review my questions during the break and I would appreciate another ten minutes, perhaps, with this witness. Because Mr. Cvijetic will not examine at all. And if I need, I will need only a little -- I'll just organise a little during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. So we take the break, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness comes in, I don't have any more questions for this witness. But since we learned only yesterday about that alleged meeting to which delegation was sent from Kozarac to Banja Luka, we had no time to verify that information, and this information is something that he -- the witness received from hearsay or double-hearsay, and I'm not in a position to ask him questions about this meeting. I have no other questions to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. And, Mr. Cvijetic, you confirm that you decline cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And will there be any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to cover some areas that were raised during cross-examination that might be useful for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, while you were on your way in, counsel for Zupljanin indicated that he, in fact, has no further questions of you so his cross-examination is complete. And counsel for Mr. Stanisic has confirmed that he doesn't intend to cross-examine. So I invite Mr. Olmsted to re-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, during cross-examination, you stated that Srdjo Srdic was replaced by Simo Miskovic at some stage as the leader of the SDS in Prijedor. Can you tell us what was Miskovic's relationship like with the SDS in Sarajevo, from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, Your Honours, because Miskovic was not in the statement parliament and Srdic was. I also had an opportunity to travel with Srdic and to spend time with him at the parliament but not with Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen 2D128.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these are the minutes of the extraordinary session of Prijedor Municipal Assembly held on 17th of February, 1992. Sir, it is clear from these minutes and also from what Mr. Aleksic read into the record yesterday that the debate, or one of the main issues in the debate, was whether a proposal for the dissolution of the assembly, the Prijedor Assembly should be placed on the agenda. Can you tell what was the position of the SDS leadership Simo Miskovic, Milomir Stakic, with regard to the dissolution of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS, vigorously advocated the dissolution of the assembly, not only at this session but even months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's also clear from the minutes that the SDA and HDZ leadership were not in favour of dissolving the assembly at that point in time. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was their position because dissolving that legitimate organ with the prevailing atmosphere, it would have been impossible to either hold new elections or form a new assembly. And the SDS, at the time of this session, of which we have the transcript, had already established its own assembly, a para-state Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I was reading through the minutes last night and I noticed there was talk about republican-wide elections being held later that year. Was that another reason why there was really no need to hold a by-election at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was another reason not to hold elections within such a short time because the presidents of the political parties, Karadzic, Izetbegovic and others, had agreed to hold elections within a year. That was by the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During examination-in-chief, you stated that even though there was this disagreement between the SDS and the other parties with regard to division of power within the municipality, that the government in Prijedor was still able to function. The assembly was still able to meet. Given that state of affairs, was there really a need to dissolve the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as the operation of the assembly is concerned, Your Honours, it had all the necessary conditions to work and it could work normally with the consent of the SDS as it had worked previously for months. All the prestigious but followed sessions were convened, sessions were held. The very fact that the secondary departments of power had not been distributed did not block the work of the assembly. The assembly was a legitimate organ and it sat in its full composition. Also the municipal government functioned in the same way, in its full composition or, rather, the Executive Board as we called it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 13 of the B/C/S of this document, page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we see after Miskovic speaks we see that someone by the name of Islam Bahonjic speaks. Who was Mr. Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Islam Bahonjic was a municipal deputy and a member of the broader SDA leadership in Prijedor and he also went to negotiate in Prijedor to those negotiation meetings when the takeover happened. And he is one of the men who never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, he asks what I believe is a relevant question. He says: "We all know that the SDS has created its own assembly so why this interest in dissolving this civilian assembly?" Now you have already just mentioned that it was -- you were aware in the media, from the media, that the SDS had created its own assembly. Was this question that Mr. Bahonjic posed in the minds of many of the non-Serb representatives at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the point of all this session and all the debates with the SDS. It was obvious to all of us. The SDS wanted to dissolve the assembly, did not want to allow a new assembly to be formed. They wanted to proclaim a state of emergency and to impose their own authorities they had already prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I would like to ask one clarification question. Mr. Witness, you speak about Islam Bahonjic who went to negotiate -- to those negotiation meetings when the takeover happened. And is he one of the men who never returned. I seem to remember that yesterday you spoke about two meetings, one they came back from, and a second one, they never returned from. That's right. But I seem to remember that you were talking then about a meeting in Banja Luka and now you say it's in Prijedor. Can you clarify which one of the two? Where -- where -- where were those meetings held? In Prijedor or in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, that is Islam Bahonjic, the man from the minutes, he was present at the second meeting in Prijedor and this delegation was led by the chief of the police, and Bahonjic was a member of that delegation together with some other people. After this second meeting, this delegation never returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And was the first meeting held from Prijedor as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first meeting with the police was also held in Prijedor. It was also led by the chief of police, and they were allowed to come back to Kozarac, and then on the second occasion, neither he returned, nor anybody in that delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps can I clarify this issue with regard to the Banja Luka meeting, if I show him a document that's on the Defence's exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't ask him any questions about this topic. I didn't use a document. I don't think this is the right way to go about this. I believe the Prosecution doesn't have the right to use these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm simply doing this as an aid for the Trial Chamber, but I am at a bit of a disadvantage here because the Defence have decided not to cross-examine on this issue of the Banja Luka meeting and I want to have this witness be able to clarify this issue so perhaps we don't have to call him back a second time to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And this relates to the adjudicated fact in respect of which this witness was called?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It is relating to events in May 1992 leading up to the shelling in Kozarac. These are -- this is the ultimatum that was finally issued that resulted in the shelling. So this time-period is -- I can actually give the facts, if Your Honours believe it is necessary. But it comes directly out of his examination-in-chief as well. Just for the record, I'm referring to this meeting in Banja Luka in which Stojan Zupljanin participated in. And Judge Delvoie's question, he was trying to clarify the Prijedor meetings versus the Banja Luka meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, that question was never raised in cross-examination and no document was shown. Of course, His Honour Judge Delvoie asked the question, and the witness may respond without being shown any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The question that the Chamber had asked didn't touch on this particular issue of this meeting in Banja Luka. So, therefore, this isn't something that arises out of cross-examination. So let's move on Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may just clarify one matter with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, the -- during your examination-in-chief, you mentioned there was a meeting in Banja Luka as well. Is that separate from these Prijedor meetings? That's all I'm asking, just to clarify whether there was another meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same objection. We have the decision of the Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You need not answer that question Mr. -- yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked during cross-examination where you actually -- read to you some of your former testimony regarding the presence of the police during cleansing operations in the Kozarac area following the shelling. And I want to draw your attention to your testimony in the Stakic case. This is at transcript page 4709. And you're talking about these operations, and you state that: "During each of these operations they killed several people. Almost as a rule in a group of 30 houses, there would -- as a rule be two or three victims," et cetera. Then later on, Ms. Korner asks you: "You talk about they, the Serbs, who do mean by that? Was this army or police or a mixture of both?" And you responded: "I mean all of them." Do you stand by that -- that answer?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do, sir. We saw them wearing various different kinds of uniforms and in different locations. On one occasion during this process of ethnic cleansing in the Trnopolje and Omarska camps, and in Prijedor after the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen 65 ter 466. Sir, during cross-examination you were shown two decisions by the Prijedor government from June of 1992 and you were asked a number of questions regarding the relationship between the Prijedor government and the ARK regional government. And I want you to take a look at this decision, number 18, which is on the organisation and work of the Prijedor Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that it's dated 20 May 1992. And if we look at Article 11, which is on this page, it says: "The provisions of the constitution, the law, and decision [sic] adopted by the Assembly, the Presidency and ... government of the Serbian Republic of BH ... and the responsible organs of the Autonomous Region of the Banja Luka Krajina have been and shall remain the foundation for the work of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff." So, sir, at least in May 1992, there was no conflict, at least no apparent conflict, between the Prijedor authorities and the ARK authorities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. In my early evidence, I said what I heard about this conflict, and I believe that in one of my testimonies I said what Kupresanin had told me; namely, that it was difficult for him to get a document for me to leave the area. And it was then that I realised that he was in a political conflict, and I think I can say literally with Vukic, with Brdjo, as he called him, or Brdjanin, and with Zupljanin. He needed to get a document for me from the police, but the recommendation for me was not to seek this document from the police, instead he gave me this document with the seal of the practically non-existent Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P555. And, Your Honours, I believe that last document is in the law library as well. If not, of course, it should be added to it. This document is a dispatch from CSB Banja Luka to all SJB chiefs dated 4 May 1992, and I just want you to take a look at item 1 through which the CSB Banja Luka conveys the decision by the ARK government that the full and public mobilisation on the entire territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is hereby ordered. Sir, do you recall in May 1992 hearing announcements to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you said you heard it through the media. Who was issuing these announcements?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Banja Luka TV, and you could also hear it on local radio stations. But I know that this was announced on several occasions on television. I don't know in what form. And also on the radio stations. I can't quote what exactly was said, but we know that there was order for general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at number 4, the CSB Banja Luka conveys the ARK government's decision that a curfew is to be introduced. Do you recall hearing announcements on the Prijedor local radio to that effect as well?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a curfew was introduced. I believe it might have been even a day or two before the 4th of May that a curfew was introduced in the Prijedor area, and it was in place until further notice. It was not abolished until the attack on Hambarine and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at 65 ter 10216. And, again, Your Honours, this should be a document is that in the law library. This is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And if we could turn to page 6 of the B/C/S, page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what's the tab number of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There is no tab. This is a document that I brought up in response to your cross-examination regarding the relationship between the ARK and the Prijedor government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want you to take a look at decision number 45. It states: "The proper municipal organs of administration shall be informed of all abandoned property, which shall then be proclaimed property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipal assemblies." And if we look at the end of this decision, it's numbered 03-513/92 and it's dated 19 June 1992. If we could now look at 65 ter 492. This is tab 12. And this is a proposal for a decision on proclaiming abandoned property, property of the state, and it's from 1992. In the first paragraph it states that: "This decision is made pursuant to, among other laws, the decision of the Crisis Staff of the ARK number 03-513/92 dated 19 June 1992." And under item number 1 it states: "All abandoned property (real estate and moveable items) of persons who have left the territory of Prijedor municipality, and of persons who participated in the armed uprising is temporarily proclaimed state property, the Prijedor municipality becoming entitled to all possession rights." After the attack on Kozarac, do you recall hearing announcements to this effect over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some practical things that happened in the field which confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you explain that just briefly to us.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here's a specific example: During the last mop-up operations, the army seized certain property, cars or tractors, and in some cases they issued papers to the owners, saying that this was an order to seize their property and that it had been issued by the municipality. I know that some people received such documents. And soon in Trnopolje, the Serbian forces approved very near the camp certain Serbian families to move into the houses of people who were only 500 metres away in the camp with their families. This wasn't spontaneous. During the time that I was in the field, they had already moved into several houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned "some people." To your knowledge, were there any Serbs who had their property confiscated after they left the municipality pursuant to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. There weren't. Only -- it related only to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, an intervention for the transcript. 42, line 3: [In English] "... that it had been issued by the municipality." [Interpretation] I believe the witness said, "I don't know who issued this." And as for tendering this document, this is a proposed decision. There is no date, there's no seal, there's no signature, that's one thing. It's only a draft. And the second thing, this document and the one shown before are not identical; for example, Article 1 which Mr. Olmsted read. So I oppose tendering this document. We have the testimony of the witness about what his knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, these arguments seem to go to weight. This witness was able to testify that he did hear this type of decision announced over the radio. He also knows that it was implemented and he gave examples of its implementation. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's the testimony. But if -- as Mr. Aleksic says, this is only a draft. So wouldn't that be admitting it -- isn't that an attempt to give it a higher status than it, in fact, has?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again that's an issue of weight. This witness says that he heard this kind of decision issued over the public radio and, therefore, that -- we would contend indicates that the decision was, in fact, passed and implemented. Because otherwise it wouldn't be announced over the radio, it wouldn't have been implemented in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness wasn't saying this for this document but the previous document which is already in the law library. And also, I didn't pursue this line of questioning. It would be very general. I didn't go into this specific line of questions. If that's how we understand things, then Mr. Olmsted could take this entire Official Gazette and show every single document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue at stake here is whether there was co-operation between the ARK government and the government in Prijedor. There -- this document is directly linked to an ARK Crisis Staff decision that I showed this witness previously. This one we agree is a proposal. It's a draft. However, because it was announced publicly at some stage, it, therefore, must have become -- or, at least, we're going contend that it became official and this simple corroborates the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have the witness's testimony. It is not necessary -- without ruling definitively on the objections made by Mr. Aleksic, this document would not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I beg the Trial Chamber's indulgence to mark it for identification in the event that we can use it for another witness who will perhaps know more and be able to authenticate it further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The evidential problem remains that it is only a draft and whereas arguments could be made as to the -- what weight should be attached to it, I would suggest -- well, I should say it seems to me, Mr. Olmsted, that as the Prosecution's case winds up, you find there's a witness in respect of whom this document could be usefully used, then we could return to it. But I don't see the need to even mark it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, just one more topic I want to cover very briefly with you. You were asked a few questions regarding the expansion of the Kozarac TO and I want to see if we can clarify the time-line here. Now, you have testified regarding this meeting in mid-May with the SDS leadership and others at which this ultimatum was issued to surrender weapons or -- and other things, or, as Commander Zeljaja stated, Kozarac would be flattened. Now, after this meeting, you've testified that you returned to Kozarac, and you conveyed this ultimatum to the leadership in Kozarac. My question for you is: Is this when the decision was made to expand the TO, to start going around and getting lists of volunteers to determine whether it's possible to increase the size of the TO to provide a defence?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the period when intensive activities were underway to turn the TO into a proper establishment. The establishment of the TO practically started the same day when we returned from the meeting at which the ultimatum was issued. We didn't even manage to finish this list. There was no time and there was no opportunity to go visit somebody for a second time and ask for their consent. You could notice about the lists that a certain number of people were said not to be at home. There was no time to go back the next day or the day after and see whether that particular person was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. Your testimony is at an end, and you're now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is it still your position that we should still try and have an extended session this afternoon with Witness ST-258?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I would ask Ms. Pidwell to speak to that. She can address it more competently that I can, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Pidwell. Can you help us out?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's really a matter for -- it's really hard to estimate how long Defence will be in their cross-examination of this witness. I anticipate I will be no longer than a session. He is only speaking to two adjudicated facts. The Defence previously -- or have stipulated to three of them, so the OTP original estimate is now reduced. He has never testified before. So it's hard to predict how he'll go. But I'm not aware -- well, Mr. Krgovic indicated earlier that his cross-examination may take a session. I don't know if he is able to provide any more of an assistance in the estimates at this stage, because there has been no change in circumstances since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, what are you -- what are your estimates?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't give you accurate estimate. I looked through the statements of this witness, and he is constantly changing them. In August of 2010, he changed what he had said before. I see now in the proofing note he said something other than what he had said in August. So a lot will depend on what he is going to say in court. You might have noticed that we do our -- that we focus our cross-examination depending on the relevance of a witness. I believe that this witness is more relevant to the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, so I will try and talk to my learned friend, Mr. Krgovic, so that he would do most of the cross-examination, and if anything remains uncovered, then I might have some questions, but I can't confirm to you that I won't have any questions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Inasmuch as there is a courtroom available this afternoon, from what counsel on both side versus indicated, it seems that we should begin, on the assumption that there is a real likelihood that we could, with the one extended session this afternoon, complete this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would have the extra session this afternoon. But the first step is that we have been alerted that an application is to be made in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To make assurance doubly sure, counsel for the Defence are agreed on the extra session this afternoon, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we finish earlier, the problem is if we go beyond that one session. I don't know how long I will take. It depends on the answers the witness will provide. I went through the application for protective measures, and again I see that the Prosecutor has expanded the application. The witness will speak to two adjudicated facts only. Now, the Prosecutor, in his application for protective measures, states that the witness would testify to other facts as well, so it is very difficult for me to tell.
